definition: A technique where third-party tracking scripts are disguised as first-party content by using DNS CNAME records to redirect requests through the website's own domain.
metaDescription: Learn about CNAME cloaking, a tracking technique that bypasses ad blockers by disguising third-party trackers as first-party content.
simpleExplanation: CNAME cloaking is like putting a fake label on a package. Websites use it to make tracking scripts from other companies look like they're coming from their own website, which helps them bypass ad blockers and privacy tools.
whyItMatters: This technique makes it harder for users to block unwanted tracking and can bypass privacy protections. It reduces transparency about what third-party services are actually collecting your data when you visit websites.
technicalDetail: CNAME cloaking works by setting up a CNAME DNS record that points a subdomain (like analytics.example.com) to a third-party tracking service. When browsers make requests to this subdomain, they treat it as first-party traffic, allowing trackers to bypass same-site policies and many ad blockers that rely on domain-based filtering.

examples.explanation: A website creates a subdomain 'stats.mysite.com' that secretly redirects to Google Analytics, making the tracking appear as if it's coming from their own domain instead of Google's servers.
An e-commerce site uses 'cdn.shop.com' to mask requests to Facebook's tracking pixel, allowing them to collect data even when users have blocked Facebook domains.
